title: PlayerControls.cs
summary: Overlay state (tasks, pause, dialogue, quest journal, minigame), the HUD button wiring, and the stress meter with its critical-stress countdown.

notes.text: Runs before PlayerMovement every frame, so the 'is something open' flags are already up to date when movement reads them.
Unity adds PlayerInputBindings automatically and refuses to remove it — PlayerControls reads every action through it.
One of three components on the Player (with PlayerInputBindings and PlayerMovement). This one owns overlay state and stress; the other two own input lookup and movement.
One flag per full-screen overlay. Public so PlayerMovement, NPCInteractionManager, the Quest and the minigames can read or set them directly.
Set by a minigame while it is on screen. Movement and the cursor freeze, NPC prompts hide, and the Quest pauses the episode timer while this is true.
Resting tint of the HUD buttons; the active tint is hudButtonActiveColor below.
Inspector group header for the stress settings.
Current stress. It does not rise by itself any more — only dialogue choices, quests and minigames move it, through ChangeStress().
The cap. Reaching it starts the critical-stress countdown.
How many seconds the player can stay at maximum stress before the stress game-over appears.
Read by the Stress HUD to show its warning state.

notes.match: public float CriticalStressRemaining { get; private set; }
notes.text: Seconds left on the countdown; 0 whenever stress is below the cap.

notes.match: [Header("HUD References — assign the real UI objects here")]
notes.text: Everything below is assigned in the Inspector (the Tools ▸ Build HUD menu items do this for you) rather than found by name at runtime.
The two HUD buttons: Tasks and Menu.
Background images that get tinted to show which panel is open.
Cached once in Awake; null-checked later because an action can be missing from a custom rebinding.
Grabs the input bindings from the same GameObject.
Wire the HUD buttons to the same toggle methods the keyboard calls.
The Menu button hands off to PauseMenu, which owns pausing.
Check the key, then update stress, then refresh the HUD — the order matters so the HUD never shows last frame's state.
Runs the max-stress countdown every frame.

notes.match: // ESC / pause is handled by PauseMenu.cs
notes.text: Only the Tasks key lives here; Esc belongs to PauseMenu.
Called by the Tasks HUD button and by the T key.
Opening Tasks closes the Quest Journal first — only one full-screen panel at a time. Null-safe because cutscene scenes have no journal.
Flip the flag, and close pause so the panels never overlap.
Public so a conversation or cutscene can force Tasks closed.
The single question gameplay asks: is anything covering the game? Movement, camera look and the cursor all check this.

notes.match: return tasksOpen || pauseOpen || dialogueOpen || questOpen || minigameOpen;
notes.text: Any one of these freezes the player. Add a new overlay by adding its flag here.
The one public entry point for anything that should move stress: dialogue choices, quests, minigames.
Clamped, so stress can never go below 0 or above the max.
Dropping back below the cap cancels the countdown and re-arms the game-over.
The 'stay at maximum for too long' rule.
Not at the cap: reset everything and do nothing.
The game-over fires once; after that this method stays quiet until stress drops.
First frame at the cap: start the countdown.
Unscaled time, so it still counts if something else changes Time.timeScale.
Countdown reached zero: show the stress game-over screen through the quest HUD.
Applies the current flags to the HUD objects. Called whenever something changes and once per frame.
Show or hide the dim overlay behind the Tasks panel.
The whole HUD hides while the pause menu is up.
Tint each HUD button to show which panel is currently open.
Show or hide the legacy Tasks panel directly.
